name: Change Audit — Windows Network Share Created, Modified or Deleted
description:
Change objective
Audit creation, modification and deletion of Windows network shares (and share permissions) for change control — new shares can expose data or enable lateral movement.

Detection logic
Windows logs share create/modify/delete with the share name/path and the acting subject. This rule surfaces all share changes as an auditable change feed.

Why this works
Share change events are low-volume and structured, giving a clean change-audit trail for a control that directly affects data exposure.

False positives
Legitimate administrative share management or software installation that creates shares.

Tuning
Correlate each share change with a ticket; escalate new shares on servers hosting sensitive data or unusual share paths.

Required telemetry
Windows Security: event.code 5142 (share created), 5143 (share/permissions modified), 5144 (share deleted); winlog.event_data.ShareName, ShareLocalPath, SubjectUserName.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation / audit guide
1. event.code = create/modify/delete; ShareName/ShareLocalPath = the share; SubjectUserName = actor.
2. Confirm authorization; a new share on a sensitive server, or a permission change opening a share, is higher priority.
false_positives: Legitimate administrative share management or software installation that creates shares.

name: Change Audit — Windows Privileged Group Membership Changed
description:
Change objective
Audit additions to and removals from privileged Windows/AD groups (Administrators, Domain/Enterprise Admins, built-in Operators, Remote Desktop/Management Users, DnsAdmins) for change control.

Detection logic
Membership changes to privileged groups grant or remove significant access. This rule surfaces every add/remove on the privileged group set as an auditable change, complementing the attack-focused Tier-0 addition detection.

Why this works
Group-membership event codes record the group, the member and the actor; scoping to privileged group names/SIDs yields a high-value, low-volume change-audit trail.

False positives
Authorized administration and role rotation.

Tuning
Correlate each change with a change/access-request ticket; additions are higher priority than removals; the attack-focused Tier-0 rule handles the critical additions at high severity.

Required telemetry
Windows Security: event.code 4728/4732/4756 (add), 4729/4733/4757 (remove); TargetUserName/TargetSid (group), MemberName/MemberSid (member), SubjectUserName (actor).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation / audit guide
1. event.code = add/remove; TargetUserName = the privileged group; MemberName = who was added/removed; SubjectUserName = actor.
2. Verify against an access-request/change ticket; correlate additions with the member's subsequent privileged activity.
false_positives: Authorized administration and role rotation.
query: event.code:("4728" or "4729" or "4732" or "4733" or "4756" or "4757") and (winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:(*Admins or *Administrators or *Operators or "Remote Desktop Users" or "Remote Management Users" or DnsAdmins or "Group Policy Creator Owners") or winlog.event_data.TargetSid:("S-1-5-32-544" or "S-1-5-32-548" or "S-1-5-32-549" or "S-1-5-32-550" or "S-1-5-32-551" or "S-1-5-32-552"))

name: Change Audit — Windows System Time Changed by an Interactive Account
description:
Change objective
Audit changes to a host's system clock by an interactive account — time changes can disrupt logging/forensics, Kerberos, and time-sensitive banking processes.

Detection logic
Windows logs system-time changes with the acting subject. Routine changes are made by the time service under machine/SYSTEM context; a change made under an interactive (human) account is a notable, auditable configuration change.

Why this works
Excluding machine/service accounts isolates human-driven time changes, which are rare and worth reviewing.

False positives
A legitimate administrator correcting the clock; a VM time-sync event under an unusual account.

Tuning
Allowlist verified time-administration; correlate with the host's time-sync configuration.

Required telemetry
Windows Security: event.code 4616; winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName, PreviousTime, NewTime.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation / audit guide
1. SubjectUserName = who changed the clock; PreviousTime/NewTime show the shift.
2. A large or unexplained time change under a human account can indicate anti-forensics or misconfiguration — verify.
false_positives: A legitimate administrator correcting the clock; a VM time-sync event under an unusual account.
query: event.code:"4616" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:("*$" or "LOCAL SERVICE" or "SYSTEM" or "NETWORK SERVICE")

name: Change Audit — Windows User Account Created/Deleted/Enabled/Disabled/Modified
description:
Change objective
Audit every Windows user-account lifecycle change (create, delete, enable, disable, rename, unlock, modify) for change-control review.

Detection logic
Windows Security logs each account-management action with the acting subject and the target account. This rule surfaces all account lifecycle changes across the estate as an auditable change feed.

Why this works
The account-management event codes are a complete, structured record of user-account changes; scoping to them yields a clean change-audit trail.

False positives
All routine helpdesk/IT account administration — this is an audit feed, expected to be non-zero.

Tuning
Route to a change-audit dashboard rather than paging; correlate each change with a change ticket; escalate creations of privileged or service accounts.

Required telemetry
Windows Security: event.code 4720 (created), 4726 (deleted), 4722 (enabled), 4725 (disabled), 4738 (changed), 4767 (unlocked), 4781 (renamed); winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName (actor), TargetUserName (target).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation / audit guide
1. event.code = the change; SubjectUserName = actor; TargetUserName = the account changed.
2. Confirm the change maps to an authorized ticket; a new/enabled account, especially privileged, is highest priority.
3. Correlate with the actor's logon and the target account's subsequent activity.
false_positives: All routine helpdesk/IT account administration — this is an audit feed, expected to be non-zero.

name: Windows — Account Sign-In Succeeded After Repeated Failures
description: The same source IP failed network sign-in (4625, type 3) for the SAME human account three or more times and then SUCCEEDED (4624, type 3) within 30 minutes — an account whose password was guessed/brute-forced from that origin. Machine accounts (*$) are excluded from THIS specific analytic because NBI telemetry demonstrated the observed fail->success pattern for machine accounts was recurring benign machine-account retry behaviour (e.g. NIM-PY-APV1$), while AD machine-account passwords are automatically managed high-entropy credentials; machine-account credential abuse remains covered by separate account/host-compromise analytics. The auth-aggregator infrastructure is also excluded. This is the compromise companion to the spray primary: it fires regardless of spray breadth, catching a targeted crack even against a single account. Ordered fail->fail->fail->success (EQL sequence) is required so a one-off typo-then-correct does not match.
note:
### Investigation — sign-in succeeded after repeated failures
1. **WHO / TO WHAT** `winlog.event_data.TargetUserName` — the account that failed repeatedly then succeeded; `source.ip` the origin; `host.name` the target.
2. **DID WHAT** >=3 failed network sign-ins then a success for the same account+source in 30m = likely a guessed/brute-forced password.
3. **WHY suspicious** a legitimate user rarely fails 3+ times then succeeds; correlate with the spray primary (was this source also spraying other accounts?).
4. **Escalate**: treat the account as potentially compromised — force a password reset, review what the account did after the success (4672/5140/5145, lateral movement). Rule out a known bad-password loop that finally synced (a service/scheduled task with a stale password).
query:
sequence by source.ip, winlog.event_data.TargetUserName with maxspan=30m
  [ any where event.code == "4625" and winlog.event_data.LogonType == "3" and not winlog.event_data.TargetUserName like "*$" and winlog.event_data.TargetUserName != "ANONYMOUS LOGON" and not cidrMatch(source.ip, "10.11.15.0/24", "10.11.101.0/24", "10.11.102.0/24") ]
  [ any where event.code == "4625" and winlog.event_data.LogonType == "3" ]
  [ any where event.code == "4625" and winlog.event_data.LogonType == "3" ]
  [ any where event.code == "4624" and winlog.event_data.LogonType == "3" ]

name: Windows — Audit Policy Changed by Interactive Account
description: Detects a change to the Windows system audit policy (4719) made by an interactive/human account rather than a computer account or SYSTEM. Routine audit-policy events come from GPO reapplication under machine/SYSTEM context (0 interactive baseline over 30d). A human changing audit policy typically means an attacker disabling audit subcategories to blind the SOC, or an unauthorised configuration change.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SubjectUserName` = the interactive account; `AuditPolicyChanges` shows which subcategory was added/removed (removal = auditing disabled).
2. Any interactive audit-policy change is unexpected — confirm against change control.
## Response
If unauthorised, restore the audit policy (GPO/`auditpol`) and investigate the account for compromise.

description: Identifies instances where an unusual process spawns a chrome browser child process. This behavior could be related to malware stealing browser information.

## Coverage

name: Windows — Credential Dumping via Reg.exe
description: Fires when reg.exe is run with save or export against the SAM, SECURITY, or SYSTEM registry hives — the technique for dumping the hives that contain local password hashes and LSA secrets for offline credential extraction. Attackers copy these hives to crack credentials away from the endpoint. The rule matches the reg.exe process arguments. Maps to ATT&CK Credential Access T1003.002 (OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager).
note:
### Investigation
1. Read process.command_line to confirm which hives were saved and where the output was written.
2. Identify the actor (user.name) and host, and whether this user/host performs sanctioned backup/imaging.
3. Inspect process.parent.name — a shell/PowerShell/unknown parent is more suspicious than a known backup tool.
4. Correlate for the output file being read/exfiltrated and for other credential-access activity on the host.
5. Escalate on non-backup context, an unusual parent, or SAM+SYSTEM saved together (the crack-ready pair).

### False positives / benign
Backup and migration tooling occasionally exports SYSTEM/SOFTWARE hives. Distinguish real credential theft by the hive set (SAM plus SYSTEM together is the crack-ready combination, rarely needed by backups), the parent process (sanctioned backup agent versus ad-hoc shell), the actor, and where the output goes. Investigate the context rather than allowlisting reg.exe, a legitimate binary the attacker deliberately abuses (LOLBin).

### Notes
Pending Batch-2 repair: bind the endpoint/4688 index (currently empty) so the rule fires; process.command_line ~52% populated (coverage cap). Local execution: the host IS the origin (no source.ip).
query: process.name : "reg.exe" AND process.args : ("save" OR "export") AND process.args : ("SAM" OR "SECURITY" OR "SYSTEM")

name: Windows — Credential Theft: Registry Hive or NTDS.dit Extraction
description:
Attacker objective
Steal the credential stores directly: the SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM registry hives (local secrets) or NTDS.dit (the entire domain credential database).

Attack logic
Attackers copy the registry hives with reg.exe save, or extract NTDS.dit using ntdsutil IFM, esentutl, diskshadow or a shadow copy, to harvest all account hashes offline.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the extraction commands. Matching hive-save and NTDS-extraction patterns isolates this theft, independent of case.

False positives
A backup or migration process that legitimately exports hives or NTDS (rare and should be scheduled/known).

Tuning
Allowlist verified backup/migration tooling and windows; treat interactive extraction as an incident.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688. NTDS.dit extraction is highest-impact on a Domain Controller.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the host, user and command line; on a Domain Controller, NTDS.dit extraction means full domain credential compromise.
2. Isolate the host; if NTDS was extracted, plan a domain-wide credential reset including a double KRBTGT rotation.
3. Locate the output file and any exfiltration.
false_positives: A backup or migration process that legitimately exports hives or NTDS (rare and should be scheduled/known).
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*save*" AND cl LIKE "*hklm*" AND (cl LIKE "*sam*" OR cl LIKE "*security*" OR cl LIKE "*system*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*ntdsutil*" AND (cl LIKE "*ifm*" OR cl LIKE "*create full*" OR cl LIKE "*ac i ntds*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*esentutl*" AND cl LIKE "*ntds*")
   OR cl LIKE "*ntds.dit*"
   OR cl LIKE "*diskshadow*"
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Windows — Defender / EDR / Firewall Tampering
description:
Attacker objective
Disable or blind endpoint defenses — Microsoft Defender, the EDR sensor, or the host firewall — to evade detection before further action.

Attack logic
Attackers disable real-time protection, add exclusions, remove signatures, stop the AV/EDR service, unload minifilter drivers, or turn off the host firewall.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the tamper commands (Set-MpPreference, MpCmdRun, service stop of the defender/EDR services, netsh firewall off, fltmc unload), independent of case.

False positives
An administrator legitimately reconfiguring Defender or the firewall during maintenance.

Tuning
Correlate with change control; allowlist sanctioned management automation identities; investigate unexpected actors.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the host/user and the exact tamper command.
2. Verify against change control; unexplained defense-tampering is a strong pre-attack indicator — treat the host as suspect.
3. Check whether protection was re-enabled and hunt for activity in the blind window.
false_positives: An administrator legitimately reconfiguring Defender or the firewall during maintenance.
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*set-mppreference*" AND cl LIKE "*disable*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*add-mppreference*" AND cl LIKE "*exclusion*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*set-mppreference*" AND cl LIKE "*exclusion*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*mpcmdrun*" AND cl LIKE "*removedefinitions*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*stop*" AND (cl LIKE "*windefend*" OR cl LIKE "*wdnissvc*" OR cl LIKE "*sense*" OR cl LIKE "*mssense*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*netsh*" AND cl LIKE "*advfirewall*" AND cl LIKE "*state off*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*netsh*" AND cl LIKE "*firewall*" AND cl LIKE "*opmode*" AND cl LIKE "*disable*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*fltmc*" AND cl LIKE "*unload*")
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Windows — DPAPI Master Key Backup Retrieved from a New Host
description: Event 4692 records an attempt to back up the DPAPI master key. Offensive tooling — Mimikatz `dpapi::`, SharpDPAPI and DonPAPI — triggers this event while harvesting the domain backup key in order to decrypt every user's stored browser passwords, certificates, RDP credentials and Credential Manager entries offline. JCB has a routine baseline of roughly 40 such events a day across 87 hosts, so a flat rule would be noisy; this rule instead alerts only when a **host that has not done this in 14 days** starts doing it. No existing rule covers this event code.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. Determine whether the host is a workstation performing normal credential-roaming or a server with no reason to touch DPAPI keys.
2. Review 4693 (DPAPI recovery) on the same host and account immediately afterwards — retrieval followed by mass recovery indicates credential harvesting rather than routine operation.
3. Correlate with `Windows — LSASS Memory Dump via Known Credential-Theft Tooling` and `Windows — Credential Theft: Registry Hive or NTDS.dit Extraction` for the same host.
4. If the account involved is privileged, treat the domain DPAPI backup key as potentially compromised.
false_positives: A newly built or newly imaged host performing its first credential-roaming operation.
Certificate enrolment or credential-manager migration activity.
Backup software that legitimately exercises DPAPI.

name: Windows — Event Log Cleared (All Channels)
description:
Detects clearing of a Windows event log — event 1102 for the Security log and event 104 for any other channel. Log clearing is a defence-evasion and anti-forensics action that almost always follows hands-on-keyboard activity.

**This rule exists to correct a coverage gap.** The existing custom rule 'AD/Windows — Security Event Log Cleared' searches for event 1102 in `logs-system.security-*`, but at JCB the Elastic Windows integration routes 1102 and 104 into the `system.application` and `system.system` datasets, not `system.security`. That rule therefore cannot fire. This rule searches all three system datasets, which is where the events actually land (validated: 16 x 1102 and 971 x 104 over 90 days).
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. `winlog.channel` identifies which log was cleared; `winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName` (1102) identifies who cleared it.
2. Reconstruct what the account did **before** the clear using every other telemetry source — the local log is by definition gone. Use FortiGate traffic, share access on other hosts, and the account's activity on the domain controllers.
3. Log clearing on the Exchange servers at JCB has a small routine baseline; log clearing anywhere else, or by an interactive user account, should be escalated.
4. Correlate with `Windows — Defender / EDR / Firewall Tampering` and `Windows — Elastic Agent Service Terminated` on the same host.

### Follow-up
Retire or fix the older 'AD/Windows — Security Event Log Cleared' rule so the SOC is not relying on a query that cannot match.
false_positives: Scheduled log maintenance or log rotation. The Entra/AD Connect server hq-adsync-app-p clears its Application log routinely (68 events in 7 days) and is excluded in the query; Exchange has a small 1102 baseline that is deliberately NOT excluded.
Server rebuilds and imaging.
Diagnostic work by administrators who clear a noisy log before reproducing a fault.
query: event.code:("1102" or "104") and not (event.code:"104" and host.name:"hq-adsync-app-p" and winlog.channel:"Application")

name: Excessive User Account Lockouts
description: Detects excessive user account lockouts (brute force indicator)
query:
FROM logs-* | WHERE event.code == "4740" 
| WHERE user.name NOT LIKE "*$" AND user.name NOT LIKE "svc_*"
| STATS lockout_count = count() BY user.name, host.name 
| WHERE lockout_count > 10

name: Windows — Executable or Script Written to an Administrative Share (Lateral Tool Transfer)
description: Detects a remote write of an executable, library or script onto the C$ or ADMIN$ administrative share. This is the staging half of lateral movement (ATT&CK T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer) and immediately precedes remote service or scheduled-task execution. Built on Windows Security event 5145 with the WriteData access mask, so it requires neither Sysmon nor Elastic Defend. Over the validation window the only accounts performing this were the Nessus scanner and ManageEngine, both excluded, leaving a clean zero baseline.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. `winlog.event_data.RelativeTargetName` is the file dropped, relative to the share root; `host.name` is the **destination**.
2. Recover the source IP by joining `winlog.event_data.SubjectLogonId` to event 4624 on the same host.
3. Check for execution of the dropped file: 4688/Sysmon 1 on the destination, or a new service (7045/4697) referencing it.
4. A `.exe` or `.dll` written into `System32`, `SysWOW64` or `Windows\Temp` by an interactive user account is high-confidence malicious.

### Tuning
Exclude specific deployment service accounts by name; do not remove the extension filter.
false_positives: Authenticated vulnerability scanning and agent deployment (Nessus, ManageEngine) — excluded by account.
Software distribution platforms pushing binaries over admin shares.
Backup or patch tooling staging files remotely.
query: event.code:"5145" and winlog.event_data.ShareName:(*C$ or *ADMIN$) and winlog.event_data.AccessList:*WriteData* and winlog.event_data.RelativeTargetName:(*.exe or *.dll or *.bat or *.cmd or *.ps1 or *.vbs or *.js or *.scr or *.msi or *.jar or *.hta) and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:("Nessus" or "manageengine" or "svc_nessus" or "scanuser") and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:*$

name: Windows — Ingress Tool Transfer via LOLBin
description:
Attacker objective
Download attacker tooling or a second-stage payload onto a compromised host using a trusted built-in binary (living off the land).

Attack logic
Rather than a browser, attackers fetch files with certutil, bitsadmin, mshta, curl/wget, or PowerShell download methods so the transfer blends in with system activity.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the LOLBin and its URL/output arguments; matching download-specific argument patterns isolates ingress transfers, independent of case.

False positives
An administrator or software-management process legitimately downloading with these tools.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned software-distribution hosts/accounts; review the destination URL for reputation.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Review the URL, the destination path and the requesting host/user.
2. If the source is untrusted, retrieve the downloaded file, isolate the host and hunt for execution of the payload.
false_positives: An administrator or software-management process legitimately downloading with these tools.
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*certutil*" AND (cl LIKE "*urlcache*" OR cl LIKE "*verifyctl*" OR cl LIKE "*-split*") AND cl LIKE "*http*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*bitsadmin*" AND (cl LIKE "*transfer*" OR cl LIKE "*addfile*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*mshta*" AND cl LIKE "*http*")
   OR ((cl LIKE "*curl *" OR cl LIKE "*wget *") AND cl LIKE "*http*" AND (cl LIKE "*-o*" OR cl LIKE "*-outfile*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*powershell*" AND (cl LIKE "*downloadfile*" OR cl LIKE "*downloadstring*" OR cl LIKE "*invoke-webrequest*" OR cl LIKE "*start-bitstransfer*") AND cl LIKE "*http*")
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Windows — Inhibit System Recovery (Ransomware Precursor)
description:
Attacker objective
Destroy backups and recovery options (shadow copies, boot recovery, backup catalog) so victims cannot restore — the hallmark preparation step of ransomware.

Attack logic
Before or during encryption, ransomware deletes Volume Shadow Copies, disables Windows boot recovery, and removes backup catalogs to maximize damage and prevent restoration.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records these destructive commands (vssadmin/wmic shadow delete, bcdedit recovery-off, wbadmin delete), independent of case.

False positives
A backup administrator legitimately pruning shadow storage or catalogs (should be scheduled/known).

Tuning
Allowlist verified backup automation and windows; treat interactive or unexpected execution as an active ransomware incident.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Treat as a likely in-progress ransomware event: isolate the host immediately.
2. Identify the user/parent process and any mass file modification; preserve evidence and invoke IR.
3. Check other hosts for the same command pattern (worming/estate-wide deployment).
false_positives: A backup administrator legitimately pruning shadow storage or catalogs (should be scheduled/known).
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*vssadmin*" AND cl LIKE "*delete*" AND cl LIKE "*shadow*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*vssadmin*" AND cl LIKE "*resize*" AND cl LIKE "*shadowstorage*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*wmic*" AND cl LIKE "*shadowcopy*" AND cl LIKE "*delete*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*win32_shadowcopy*" AND cl LIKE "*delete*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*bcdedit*" AND (cl LIKE "*recoveryenabled*no*" OR cl LIKE "*bootstatuspolicy*ignoreallfailures*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*wbadmin*" AND cl LIKE "*delete*" AND (cl LIKE "*catalog*" OR cl LIKE "*systemstatebackup*" OR cl LIKE "*backup*"))
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Windows — LSASS Memory Dump via Known Credential-Theft Tooling
description:
Attacker objective
Dump the memory of the LSASS process to extract plaintext credentials, hashes and Kerberos tickets.

Attack logic
LSASS holds credential material for logged-on users. Attackers dump its memory with tools such as procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, nanodump, or built-in minidump routines, then extract secrets offline.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the tool and its arguments. Matching known LSASS-dump tool/argument patterns targeting lsass isolates credential theft, independent of case.

False positives
Legitimate crash-diagnostic tooling explicitly dumping lsass (rare). A renamed dumping tool would still match on the lsass/MiniDump argument pattern.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned diagnostic hosts/accounts; treat any hands-on-keyboard lsass dump as an incident.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688 (process.command_line).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the host, user and full command line; confirm the target is lsass.
2. Treat the host as compromised: isolate, rotate credentials of all accounts logged on to that host, and begin IR.
3. Hunt for the dumped file and any exfiltration or offline-cracking follow-on.
false_positives: Legitimate crash-diagnostic tooling explicitly dumping lsass (rare). A renamed dumping tool would still match on the lsass/MiniDump argument pattern.

| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*lsass*" AND (cl LIKE "*procdump*" OR cl LIKE "*minidump*" OR cl LIKE "*nanodump*" OR cl LIKE "*dumpert*" OR cl LIKE "*sqldumper*" OR cl LIKE "*createdump*" OR cl LIKE "*rdrleakdiag*" OR cl LIKE "*avdump*"))

name: Windows — Malicious PowerShell: AMSI/ETW Bypass or Offensive Tooling
description:
Attacker objective
Run offensive PowerShell in memory — bypassing AMSI/ETW inspection, dumping credentials, roasting Kerberos, or enumerating the domain.

Attack logic
Attacker frameworks disable AMSI/ETW and load credential-theft, Kerberos-abuse, enumeration and injection modules. Script-block logging records the expanded script even when it was launched obfuscated or base64-encoded.

Why this detection works
PowerShell 4104 captures the decoded script-block text, so matching known offensive markers detects the activity despite encoding or obfuscation.

False positives
Security testing, or a defensive script that references these strings by name. Bare Net.WebClient/download usage is excluded as too common.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned red-team/testing windows; treat production hits as incidents.

Required telemetry
PowerShell Operational 4104 (script-block logging must be enabled).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Read the full script-block text to confirm intent (AMSI bypass, credential theft, enumeration).
2. Identify the host/user; if malicious, isolate and rotate credentials used on that host.
3. Correlate with process-creation, logon and outbound-network telemetry for the same host/time.
false_positives: Security testing, or a defensive script that references these strings by name. Bare Net.WebClient/download usage is excluded as too common.

### Investigating Mofcomp Activity

name: Windows — Password Spray From a Single Source
description: One source IP failed network sign-in (Windows 4625, logon type 3) against 10 or more DISTINCT accounts within an hour — the fan-out signature of password spraying. NBI's normal auth-failure baseline is dominated by stuck credentials (one source, one-two accounts) and by auth-aggregator infrastructure (the scanwave vulnerability scanner, VDI/RDS farms on 10.11.101.0/24 and 10.11.102.0/24, and app/Citrix servers on 10.11.15.0/24) which legitimately touch many accounts; those are excluded as an evidence-backed category (known_infrastructure:auth-aggregators). Keyed on DISTINCT-account cardinality per source (not raw failure volume), so a stuck-credential loop that fails one account thousands of times does NOT match, while a spray across many accounts does. source.ip is ~71% populated on 4625 (network logons carry it); local failures without a source are out of scope for this analytic.
note:
### Investigation — password spray from one source
1. **WHO / FROM WHERE** `source.ip` — is it a workstation/server that has no business attempting sign-in to many accounts? Resolve the host; a normal endpoint fails 1–2 accounts, not 10+.
2. **DID WHAT / TO WHAT** the rule fired because this source failed >=10 DISTINCT accounts in an hour. Pull the target accounts (4625 `winlog.event_data.TargetUserName` for this source) — are they enumerated/sequential or a real user population?
3. **WHY suspicious** breadth: one origin touching many identities = spray. Check `winlog.event_data.SubStatus` (0xc000006a bad-password across many users = spray; 0xc0000064 user-not-exist = enumeration).
4. **Escalate** if any of the sprayed accounts then SUCCEEDS (4624) from this source — that is a compromise (see the brute-force-success companion). De-escalate only after confirming the source is a newly-added, sanctioned auth aggregator; then add it to known_infrastructure by evidence, not as a blanket allowlist.

description:
Detects installation of a service whose name matches the remote-execution tool families used for lateral movement: Sysinternals PsExec (PSEXESVC), PAExec, RemCom, CSExec, winexe and Impacket. Uses System-channel event 7045, which records ServiceName, ImagePath and the account the service runs as. This complements the existing 4697-based image-path rule by keying on the tool's service name instead, and covers hosts where Security-channel service auditing is not enabled.

**Why new_terms rather than a plain query:** the authenticated Nessus scanner installs PSEXESVC across the estate as part of its credentialed checks — 110 events on 51 hosts in 7 days. Event 7045 carries no actor field, so the scanner cannot be excluded by account name the way it can on event 5145. Keying on a previously unseen host/service pair over a 14-day history suppresses the recurring scan targets while still alerting the first time PsExec lands on a host that has not seen it before.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. `winlog.event_data.ImagePath` shows the binary; `winlog.event_data.AccountName` shows the run-as context (usually LocalSystem).

name: Windows — Remote Execution via WMI or WinRM
description:
Attacker objective
Execute commands on a remote host over WMI or WinRM/PowerShell-Remoting to move laterally after a foothold.

Attack logic

Why this detection works
Process-creation lineage ties the WMI/WinRM host process to a suspicious child on the same event, isolating remote execution from local activity.

False positives
Legitimate remote administration and management tooling that uses WMI/WinRM.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned management/monitoring source hosts and service accounts; a burst across many destination hosts is higher-risk.

Required telemetry
Process creation with parent process: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. The parent (WmiPrvSE/wsmprovhost) launched a shell/tool — remote WMI/WinRM execution.

name: Windows — Remote SAM Enumeration via SMB Named Pipe
description: Detects remote binding to the SAMR named pipe over SMB by an interactive user account. SAMR backs the account and group enumeration performed by BloodHound/SharpHound, net.exe, rpcclient and Impacket samrdump, used to inventory domain users, groups and privileges before privilege escalation. Machine accounts and known scanner accounts are excluded because they generate this traffic routinely at JCB. Validated baseline after exclusions: 3 events across 7 days. The `lsarpc` and `netlogon` pipes were deliberately excluded from this rule — a single monitoring account generates ~230,000 lsarpc binds per week at JCB, which would render the rule unusable.

note:
### Triage
1. Confirm whether the account is an administrator performing legitimate directory work.
2. Volume matters: a single bind is routine, dozens of binds across many hosts in minutes indicates automated enumeration.
3. Pivot to `AD — Domain Reconnaissance via LOLBins / BloodHound` and PowerShell 4104 activity for the same user.
4. Check whether the same account subsequently appears in Tier-0 group changes or Kerberoasting alerts.

name: Windows — Remote Service Execution via SMB Named Pipe (PsExec / Impacket)
description: Detects remote access to the Service Control Manager (svcctl), the PsExec service pipe (PSEXESVC) or the Task Scheduler ATSVC pipe over SMB. This is the core mechanism behind PsExec, Impacket smbexec/atexec/psexec and most hands-on-keyboard lateral movement. Detection is based on Windows Security event 5145 (detailed file share access), so it works on every host that audits share access and does NOT require Sysmon or command-line auditing — both of which are only partially deployed at JCB. Known vulnerability-scanner and monitoring service accounts, and machine accounts, are excluded.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. Identify the **source** of the SMB session: correlate `winlog.event_data.SubjectLogonId` with event 4624 on the same host to recover `source.ip` and the logon type (expect Type 3 / Network).

3. Look for a matching binary drop on `C$`/`ADMIN$` — see the companion rule *Windows — Executable or Script Written to an Administrative Share*.

IT administrators using Sysinternals PsExec for legitimate remote support.

description:
Attacker objective
Create a scheduled task that runs attacker code for persistence or delayed/repeated execution.

Attack logic
Attackers register tasks that launch obfuscated PowerShell, scripting hosts, download cradles or binaries from user-writable paths, so the payload runs on a trigger or schedule.

Why this detection works
Scheduled-task-creation auditing (4698) records the full task definition; matching suspicious action/command patterns in the task content isolates malicious tasks, independent of case.

False positives
A legitimate administrative or software task that happens to invoke PowerShell with these arguments.

Tuning
Allowlist verified task authors/names; treat encoded/hidden/download tasks as high-risk.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4698 (TaskName, TaskContent).

note:
## Investigation guide

| WHERE (tc LIKE "*powershell*" AND (tc LIKE "*-enc*" OR tc LIKE "*frombase64*" OR tc LIKE "*downloadstring*" OR tc LIKE "*downloadfile*" OR tc LIKE "*invoke-expression*" OR tc LIKE "*webclient*" OR tc LIKE "*iex(*" OR tc LIKE "*iex *"))

Install a new Windows service whose image is a command interpreter, script, or a binary in a user-writable path — for persistence or remote code execution.

Attack logic
Legitimate services run vendor executables from Program Files/System32. A service configured to launch cmd/powershell, a scripting host, an encoded command, or a binary under Temp/AppData is a persistence or lateral-execution mechanism (also used by PsExec-style tools).

Service-installation auditing (4697) records the service image path; matching interpreter/encoded/user-writable-path patterns isolates malicious services, independent of case.

## Investigation guide

Attacker objective
Execute attacker code through a trusted, signed Windows binary to bypass application control and evade defenses.

Attack logic
regsvr32 (scrobj/COM scriptlets), rundll32/mshta (inline javascript/vbscript), InstallUtil and MSBuild can run attacker-supplied code while appearing as trusted system binaries.

Process command-line auditing records the proxy-execution argument patterns (scriptlet URLs, inline script protocols, uninstall-method abuse), independent of case.

Rare legitimate use of these binaries with scriptlet/inline-script arguments.

Allowlist verified administrative scripts; review the referenced scriptlet/URL.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.

| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)

name: Windows — Single Account Failing From Many Sources
description: One user account failed network sign-in (Windows 4625, logon type 3) from 5 or more DISTINCT source IPs within an hour — a distributed credential attack (password guessing / credential stuffing) against a single account, the many-sources-to-one-user pattern that the single-source spray primary does not cover. NBI baseline: normal users fail from <=4 distinct sources over a WEEK (typically their own workstation, laptop, Citrix and phone) and <=2 in any hour; only the SRLCL service account legitimately fails from many sources (a stuck/rotating password deployed on ~22 hosts, running processes via 4688) and is excluded as an evidence-backed known service account. Machine accounts (*$) are excluded from THIS analytic because their observed many-source failures are benign auto-managed-credential retry, and machine-account credential abuse is covered by separate account/host-compromise analytics. Keyed on distinct-SOURCE cardinality per account in a short window, so a legitimate multi-device user does not trip it but a coordinated attack against one identity does.
note:
### Investigation — one account attacked from many sources
1. **WHO / TO WHAT** `winlog.event_data.TargetUserName` — the account under attack. Is it a normal human user (should fail from <=4 sources/week) or a shared/service account?
2. **DID WHAT / FROM WHERE** it failed network sign-in from >=5 distinct source IPs in an hour. Pull those source IPs (4625 for this account) — internal workstations, a NAT/proxy egress, or unrelated/external hosts (distributed attack)?
3. **WHY suspicious** breadth of ORIGINS against one identity = distributed guessing/stuffing; correlate `winlog.event_data.SubStatus` (0xc000006a bad-password from many sources).
4. **Escalate** if the account then SUCCEEDS from any of those sources (see the brute-force-success companion) — treat as compromise; force a reset. De-escalate only after confirming a new legitimate shared/service account (add to known_infrastructure service accounts by evidence, not a blanket allowlist).

standard.rule_type_rationale: D0 observable = cardinality of distinct SOURCE IPs per target account crossing a baselined number; D2 (cardinality IS the behavior) -> Threshold with cardinality (key = TargetUserName, cardinality = source.ip). Companion to the source->many-users primary; different key covers the many-sources->one-user evasion.
standard.baseline: normal users <=4 distinct sources/7d, <=2/24h; threshold 5/1h; SRLCL (service, 22 sources/1h) excluded

exclusion_record.evidence: SRLCL runs processes (4688), 7/7 days, peak 22 sources/1h = stuck-password service; machine accounts auto-managed high-entropy
exclusion_record.fp_reduction: removes the only current high-cardinality account
exclusion_record.coverage_lost: a distributed attack specifically against SRLCL
exclusion_record.evasion_introduced: attacker targets SRLCL (a service account) — compensated by the fail->success correlation

standard.replaces: raad-13-per-user-distributed-spray (noisy cross-surface: o365 empty, FortiGate user null; fired on SRLCL + multi-device users)

Several trusted Windows binaries auto-elevate and can be hijacked (via registry/COM manipulation) to launch an attacker process elevated. The tell is an auto-elevating binary spawning a command interpreter or scripting host.

Process-creation lineage links the auto-elevating parent to a shell/scripting child on the same event, a combination that does not occur in normal use.

Rare legitimate automation that launches a shell from one of these binaries.

Allowlist verified parent/child pairs if a legitimate workflow triggers it.

Required telemetry
Process creation with parent process: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688 (process.parent.name).
